passage:
I'm Saurabh. Last month I promised Swati I'd come to her kho-kho final on Saturday. Then a boy in my class invited me to his birthday party at the same time, with a magic show and a big cake. I really wanted to go. My stomach felt twisted all Friday.
I kept thinking, Swati won't even notice. But I had said it. So I went to the ground.
Her team lost. She came over, sweaty and sad, and said, "You came. I looked for you before the last round." I felt proud, and also a bit sad about the cake.
Now Swati tells people, "Saurabh always turns up." I like being that person.

qa.q: What was going to be at the birthday party?
qa.a: A magic show and a big cake.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel all Friday, and why?
qa.a: Saurabh felt torn and uneasy, stomach twisted, because the promise to Swati was pulling against wanting to go to the party.

qa.q: Which choice did Saurabh make, and what did it build?
qa.a: Saurabh kept the promise and went to the ground, which built a name as someone who always turns up.

qa.q: What did it mean to Swati that Saurabh came?
qa.a: It meant a lot; she had looked for Saurabh before the last round, and even after losing she was glad the promise was kept.

grounding: A child keeps a promise to watch Swati's match even when a party pulls hard, and gains a sense of being reliable.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday.
Suraj (8) spent the afternoon helping Gautam finish a surprise card for Gautam's mother's birthday. Gautam made him promise not to tell. At pickup, Gautam's mother asked Suraj what they had been making. I watched his face go red; he was bursting. He clamped his hands over his mouth, shook his head and said, "It's a secret. I promised."
Afterwards he told me, "That was SO hard, Aunty." I told him a happy surprise is a good secret to keep, and that secrets which make someone unsafe or sad are ones to tell a grown-up. He nodded seriously and asked if he could help wrap it tomorrow.

qa.q: What were Suraj and Gautam making?
qa.a: They were making a surprise card for Gautam's mother's birthday.

qa.q: What does Suraj clamping his hands over his mouth show?
qa.a: It shows Suraj was excited and tempted to tell, but held on to his promise even though it felt SO hard.

qa.q: What did the carer explain to Suraj about secrets?
qa.a: She said a happy surprise is a good secret to keep, but secrets that make someone unsafe or sad should be told to a grown-up.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel when he hears Suraj kept the surprise?
qa.a: Gautam would likely feel relieved and trust Suraj more, knowing the surprise is still safe.

grounding: A carer watches a boy struggle to keep a promised surprise and learn that keeping his word through discomfort makes him reliable.

passage:
On Saturday morning, the school's football ground was nearly empty when Rajni arrived for the inter-school match, sweaty and out of breath.
She had promised Sahil on Monday that she would come watch his first match as goalkeeper. Then, on Friday, her best friend Meenu invited her to a birthday party with a magic show, at the same time. Rajni had spent all night wishing she could be in two places.
She stood by the fence. Her stomach felt heavy. Everyone at the party would be laughing right now.
Then Sahil saw her. He waved both gloves wildly. "You came!"
During the second half, he saved a penalty and turned to look at her, grinning.
On the way home, her mother asked, "Was it worth missing the magic show?"
Rajni thought about Sahil's face. "Yes. He knew I'd come."

qa.q: What did Sahil play as in his first match?
qa.a: He played as goalkeeper.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel standing by the fence?
qa.a: Rajni felt heavy and disappointed, still wishing she could be at the party with the magic show.

qa.q: What would you say to Rajni about her choice?
qa.a: Keeping her word even when it was inconvenient showed Sahil she is someone he can rely on.

qa.q: What was it like for Sahil when he saw Rajni by the fence?
qa.a: Sahil felt happy and supported, waving both gloves and looking to her after his penalty save.

grounding: It shows a schoolchild keeping a promise to come to a friend's match despite a more tempting invitation, building a sense of being reliable.

passage:
Monday. On the walk home, Mridul told Rekha a secret: he still slept with the light on because the dark scared him. "Promise you won't tell?" "Promise," Rekha said.
Wednesday. At lunch, the other kids were laughing about who was scared of what. "Mridul looks like someone who's scared of the dark," one boy joked. Everyone turned to Rekha, who knew Mridul best. The secret was right on her tongue, and she wanted to laugh with them. Her cheeks went hot. "No idea," she said, and took a big bite of her roti.
The next Monday, Mridul waited for her at the gate. "Rekha, can I tell you something else? I'm nervous about the swimming test."
Rekha felt something warm in her chest. He trusted her. And she knew, somehow, that she was the kind of person who kept things.

qa.q: What secret did Mridul tell Rekha on Monday?
qa.a: He still slept with the light on because the dark scared him.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when everyone turned to her at lunch?
qa.a: Rekha felt tempted and embarrassed, wanting to laugh with the group but uneasy about breaking her promise.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying "No idea" and keeping the secret worked, because Mridul's trust grew and he shared more with her.

qa.q: How does Mridul see Rekha the next Monday?
qa.a: Mridul sees her as someone safe to trust, so he tells her his worry about the swimming test.

grounding: It shows a child keeping a friend's harmless secret through temptation over several days, building reputation and an inner sense of reliability.

passage:
Trisha, you want to skip your friend's dance show because it's raining? Let your Sunaina Nani tell you about the rain of 1968.
I was ten. My friend Kamla had a small part in the temple play, just one line. I had promised to sit in the front row. That evening the sky opened. Mud everywhere. My mother said, "Stay home, she won't even notice."
I sat at the window, wanting to stay dry so badly. But I had said it. Promise. I took Father's big black umbrella and walked, my feet squelching in my chappals.
When I arrived, soaking, Kamla was peeping from behind the curtain, looking at the front row. When she saw me, she smiled so big she almost forgot her line.
After that, she always said, "Sunaina comes. Even in rain." I liked being that person. I still do.

qa.q: What did young Sunaina take to walk in the rain?
qa.a: She took Father's big black umbrella.

qa.q: How did young Sunaina feel at the window before leaving?
qa.a: She felt torn and reluctant, badly wanting to stay dry but uneasy about breaking her promise.

qa.q: At what turning point did Sunaina choose to keep her word?
qa.a: At the window, when she decided "I had said it. Promise," and walked out despite the mud.

qa.q: How did Kamla feel when she saw Sunaina in the front row?
qa.a: Kamla felt happy and relieved, smiling so big she almost forgot her line.

grounding: A grandmother recalls keeping a childhood promise through heavy rain and how it built her sense of being reliable.

passage:
Payal had promised Aditi on Monday: "I'll come to your final, I swear." Aditi was the goalkeeper, and she was terrified.
On Saturday, Nandita's birthday invite came for the same afternoon, with a magic show. And it started to pour.
"Nobody will go to a match in this," Mummy said. "Go to the party."
Payal stood at the window, pulled in two. But she kept seeing Aditi's face on Monday.
"I promised," she said. "Can you drop me at the ground?"
Mummy looked at her for a long moment and fetched the umbrella.
Payal stood on the muddy sideline for the whole match. Aditi saved two goals. At the end she ran over, soaked, and hugged Payal so hard they nearly fell.
"You came!"
Payal missed the magic show. She didn't mind as much as she had expected.

qa.q: What position did Aditi play?
qa.a: Aditi was the goalkeeper.

qa.q: How did Payal feel standing at the window?
qa.a: Payal felt pulled in two, tempted by the magic show and the easy excuse of rain, but uneasy about breaking her word.

qa.q: What did keeping the promise teach Payal?
qa.a: That her word counts even when it is hard, and that being reliable felt good and meant a lot to Aditi.

qa.q: What did it mean to Aditi that Payal came?
qa.a: Aditi, who had been terrified, felt so happy and supported that she ran over and hugged Payal in the rain.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a promise to a friend through rain and a tempting party, learning that her word binds her.
